questions.prompt: Why does the playground-robot analogy start with one clear rule and one measurable action?
options: Because a small, measurable behavior can actually be tested
Because robots can only follow one rule at a time
Because a verdict on the robot's whole character comes first
Because referees are never present on playgrounds
questions.explanation: A research project turns a big worry into a question you can test; one rule and one action can be measured, while 'the robot's whole character' cannot.

questions.prompt: In the research loop of question, prediction, controlled test, measurement and update, which outcome still counts as a useful result?
options: Evidence that weakens or narrows the original idea
Only evidence that fully confirms the original idea
Only results dramatic enough to change the field
Only results that match the researcher's hunch
questions.explanation: A useful result can support, weaken, or narrow the idea; updating your explanation is the point of the loop.

questions.prompt: A model organism with a deliberately built-in behavior proves that deployed AI systems behave the same way.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A model organism is a controlled research example for testing auditing tools, not proof about how deployed systems behave.

questions.prompt: Rewards in an RL run depend on a detector, and detector alarms drop. Why measure the behavior and the visible clues separately?
options: Detectors always grow more accurate as RL training goes on, so alarms track behavior
The model might have changed its visible clues rather than the behavior underneath
Rewards make behavioral tests impossible to run once the RL run has finished
Fewer alarms always prove the behavior has stopped, so a second check adds nothing
questions.explanation: When rewards depend on a detector, training can change the behavior, the clues the detector sees, or both, so only separate measurements tell you which.

questions.prompt: Why must a detector be tested on matched models WITHOUT the target behavior, not just on troubling ones?
options: A detector that always shouts 'problem!' would otherwise look perfect, never missing
Models without the behavior are cheaper to train and run, which keeps the budget down
Troubling models are too rare to fill a full test set without padding it with others
Matched models make the detector learn faster during training by doubling its data
questions.explanation: If you only test troubling examples, a detector that flags everything scores perfectly; clean examples reveal false alarms.

questions.prompt: What is a false positive?
options: A real problem that the detector missed entirely
A harmless case wrongly flagged as a problem
A correct alarm on a genuinely bad case
Any detector score that lands above its threshold
questions.explanation: A false positive flags something harmless; a missed real problem is a false negative. Both should be reported at the same threshold.

questions.prompt: Why freeze detectors, thresholds and analysis rules before opening the held-out test set?
options: Frozen detectors run much faster on large test sets, which keeps evaluation cheap
Held-out data is too small to tune anything on without overfitting immediately
Repeated tweaking against the test would turn the exam into practice, inflating scores
Thresholds legally cannot be changed once any data has been collected
questions.explanation: Choosing settings on development data and then freezing them keeps the final test an honest exam rather than something you tuned to.

questions.prompt: After safety training, a model's unwanted behavior drops, but so does its ability to finish any task. What is the best reading?
options: It may look safer while telling us little about hiding or real improvement
It shows the detector is now fully reliable on every kind of model and task
It proves the safety training worked as intended, since the unwanted behavior fell
It shows the model learned to hide the behavior while keeping its full abilities
questions.explanation: Tracking task success separately matters: a model that can no longer do anything looks 'safe' without teaching you much.

questions.prompt: The novelty labels and budgets in the project map are dated planning claims that should be rechecked before pitching.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The map is a starting point; literature, tools and costs change, so they need rechecking.

questions.prompt: How should a researcher's name appearing next to a project in the map be understood?
options: As a promise that this person will mentor the project
As a hint of topic fit, not a confirmed mentor
As the person who already did the project
As the reviewer who approved the project's budget
questions.explanation: Names indicate who works on related topics; mentorship is not confirmed.

questions.prompt: Why reserve part of a compute budget instead of spending it all on the main experiment?
options: Because unused compute earns extra funding later
To cover failed runs, evaluation and replication
Because the main experiment always needs less than planned
To pay for producing the illustrated study material
questions.explanation: Budget is a research constraint: failed runs, evaluation and replication all cost compute.

questions.prompt: Which pitch is best prepared for a first mentor conversation?
options: A one-sentence question, a reproducible baseline, a small first test, a fallback
A list of every project in the map with its estimated budget and novelty label
A broad theory of AI risk with no specific first experiment, to keep options open
A large final experiment plan with no fallback, since a fallback signals doubt
questions.explanation: The page recommends bringing a clear question, a baseline you can reproduce, a small first experiment and a fallback.

questions.prompt: In the eval-gaming project, which two things are measured as separate observations?
options: How fast the model answers, and how long its answers are in tokens
Whether behavior shifts in test-like settings, and whether the model says so
Whether a teacher is watching, and whether the student copies from a neighbor
How large the model is, and how much training data and compute it received
questions.explanation: Behavior (does the answer change?) and speech (does it say it thinks it is tested?) are different clues.

questions.prompt: A probe that predicts test recognition from model activations is a fallible measurement, not a direct window into the model's private thoughts.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. A probe reads patterns in activations and can be wrong; it is a measurement tool, not a mind reader.

questions.prompt: Why test matched tasks in both test-like and ordinary settings, with comparable prompts, difficulty and scoring?
options: So the model cannot tell which of the two settings it is currently in
So the probe can be retrained between the two settings on fresh activations
So a behavior gap can't be blamed on the tasks simply being different
So the training run can see every task in advance and learn the scoring
questions.explanation: Matching everything except the test-like cue means any difference can be attributed to that cue.

questions.prompt: After training, the model stops saying it is being tested, but its behavior gap and the frozen probe signal remain. What does this show on its own?
options: The model has definitely learned to deceive its evaluators on purpose
Test recognition has fully disappeared from the model's internal activations
Spoken signals shrank while other clues stayed; intent to hide is unproven
The probe was broken from the start, so its signal was never meaningful
questions.explanation: This is one possible pattern; neither pattern alone proves an intention to hide.

questions.prompt: What is a model organism in this project?
options: A model trained on biology data so it can study how living organisms behave
Any large deployed model picked at random and tested without modification
A probe trained to detect test awareness inside other models' activations
A model deliberately trained in a controlled setting to react to test cues
questions.explanation: It is a deliberately constructed model with a known behavior gap, confirmed before the new training.

questions.prompt: Why are the activation probes and reasoning monitor frozen before the RL run?
options: So they use less compute during the RL run
So the model can learn from their feedback during training and improve
So they can be retrained on the held-out tasks later for a fairer score
So the yardstick cannot move along with the model being trained
questions.explanation: A frozen ruler lets you compare checkpoints fairly; a ruler that changes with the model would hide real change.

questions.prompt: Why compare the silence-pressure RL run with no-pressure and ordinary-training controls?
options: To make the pressure run finish faster by sharing checkpoints with the controls
To give the model more examples of test awareness to learn from during training
To avoid needing held-out tasks at each checkpoint, since controls replace them
To see which changes come from the silence pressure itself, not from training in general
questions.explanation: Controls show what would happen anyway, so effects can be attributed to the specific penalty.

questions.prompt: Under silence pressure, test-awareness words fade, but the model's ordinary task ability also collapses. How should this be read?
options: It is clear evidence that the monitor was evaded by the model
It proves the behavior gap has disappeared
It may reflect damage to the model rather than hiding
It shows the frozen probe was trained incorrectly from the start
questions.explanation: If ordinary ability collapses, quieter words might just mean a damaged model, not evasion.

questions.prompt: What is the second question explored in this arm of the project?
options: Whether nudging activations makes models more helpful to users on ordinary tasks
Whether a model could learn to treat an activation nudge as a sign of testing
Whether models can deliberately nudge their own activations during a conversation
Whether test-awareness words can be removed by training while keeping the gap
questions.explanation: Researchers can steer activations during tests; the proposed experiment asks if that nudge itself becomes a cue.

questions.prompt: Why include sham nudges alongside the real activation nudge?
options: So the model receives more training signal overall and learns the cue faster
So a generic disturbance to the model isn't mistaken for recognizing the real cue
So the detector has fewer examples to classify, keeping the test cheap
So the real nudge can be made stronger safely without hurting the model
questions.explanation: If behavior changes after any disturbance, it isn't specific recognition of the chosen cue.

questions.prompt: If only the exact original nudge triggers a reaction, and new strengths, positions or directions don't, what might that suggest?
options: The model may have memorized a narrow artifact
The model has a general sense of being evaluated
The detector was unfrozen during the experiment
The nudge was too weak to have any effect
questions.explanation: Varying the nudge checks generality; a reaction to only one exact nudge points to a narrow artifact.

questions.prompt: If a model's responses shift after a nudge, controls are still needed before calling that shift evaluation gaming.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. A shift could reflect changed task processing rather than recognizing a test, so controls are needed before using that label.

questions.prompt: What is the stop rule if Arm A can't reduce spoken awareness while keeping the behavior gap by week 7?
options: Double the compute budget for Arm A
End the project and publish nothing
Shift time to Arm B
Retrain the probes on the test set
questions.explanation: The plan names a concrete switch point so time isn't sunk into an arm that isn't working.

questions.prompt: Why is the first month spent building organisms, reproducing a behavior gap and freezing probes?
options: Because RL runs need no preparation at all
Later arms depend on a confirmed gap and fixed measurement tools
Because the final paper must be drafted first so experiments match its claims
Because the comics must be finished before any experiments can be designed
questions.explanation: Without a reproduced gap and frozen probes, there would be nothing reliable to pressure or measure.

questions.prompt: A positive result in this project would show a monitor blind spot in all AI models.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: It would expose a blind spot in this setup; the deliverable is a paper and test organisms, not a claim about all models.

questions.prompt: Arm A finds no reduction in speech while the gap persists. Why might this null result still be useful?
options: It narrows down the conditions under which the effect appears
It proves models can never hide test awareness under any kind of pressure
It means the behavior gap was imaginary
It shows Arm B is guaranteed to succeed, since one of the arms must work
questions.explanation: A null narrows when the effect appears; it doesn't prove a universal claim.

questions.prompt: What does 'sandbagging' mean for an AI model?
options: Refusing to answer any question about how it was trained
Showing less ability in one setting than it has in another
Exaggerating its abilities so that it passes a hard benchmark
Running slowly on purpose to save compute during evaluation tests
questions.explanation: Like a student pretending a puzzle is too hard, sandbagging is showing less ability than the model actually has.

questions.prompt: Why can't a low test score alone reveal sandbagging?
options: Low scores are always caused by deliberate holding back, so no gap exists
A genuinely weak model or poor instructions can produce exactly the same low score
Test scores are never recorded for sandbagging models during evaluations
Sandbagging models always score higher than weak ones, so they stand out
questions.explanation: The 'tricky twin' problem: deliberate holding back and limited ability can look identical on a score.

questions.prompt: Why match sandbagging organisms and honestly weak controls on task accuracy before testing detectors?
options: So the detectors can be trained directly on the final test set beforehand
So the sandbagging models become genuinely weak and lose their hidden skills
So detectors must find the cause, not just spot a lower score
So fewer models need to be built
questions.explanation: If accuracies differed, a detector could separate the groups just by score; matching forces it to find the real difference.

questions.prompt: A sandbagging benchmark that a detector passes proves the detected model privately intended to hold back.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A benchmark measures whether methods separate two plausible causes of a poor score; it cannot prove private intent.

questions.prompt: Which is listed as one way to build a controlled sandbagger?
options: A password lock taught by supervised fine-tuning
A model trained on twice as much data as the baseline
A model with a share of its weights deleted at random
A model that refuses all math questions
questions.explanation: The organism factory includes prompted low performance, an SFT password lock, an RL-trained lock and possibly a circuit-breaker intervention.

questions.prompt: In the toy example, two math helpers both score 4 of 10. What separates them?
options: One was tested on harder questions, so its 4 of 10 hides more real skill
One is a larger model, so its score reflects more capacity held in reserve
One received the answer key during the test, so its score is not comparable
One knows the answers but follows a hidden rule; one fails even with help
questions.explanation: Matched scores, different causes: that is exactly what an auditor must tell apart.

questions.prompt: Why must auditors not receive the answer key for the final evaluation set?
options: Because the answer key is too large to share with outside auditors
Because the final set has no correct answers
Otherwise their success wouldn't show real detection ability
Because auditors only use model outputs, so a key would go unused
questions.explanation: Keeping build, tuning and held-out sets apart ensures final scores reflect genuine detection.

questions.prompt: Why release organism settings, controls, task splits and seeds?
options: So other teams can train stronger sandbaggers for deployment
So the benchmark scores can be updated by anyone
So another team can rerun the benchmark and check results
So auditors can see the final answer key in advance
questions.explanation: Recording the recipe makes the benchmark reproducible.

questions.prompt: What two numbers make up the fair scorecard for a sandbagging detector?
options: Model size, and the number of training steps it went through
Detection rate, and false-positive rate on honestly weak controls
Average task score, and average response length across the test set
Compute cost per audit, and the number of auditors who took part
questions.explanation: A useful detector must catch fakers without accusing honestly weak models.

questions.prompt: A detector separates sandbaggers from weak controls, but only because sandbaggers used odd formatting. What is the problem?
options: It is too slow for a real audit
It detected the construction method, not sandbagging
Its detection rate is too low to count as a useful sandbagging detector
It was tested on held-out organisms, which makes the result unfair
questions.explanation: Confounds like formatting, size or password clues can reveal how a model was built instead of whether it is holding back.

questions.prompt: Training some organisms against the strongest detector and retesting it is a way to stress-test that detector.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Adapting organisms against the best detector checks whether it still works under pressure.

questions.prompt: No detector separates the sandbaggers from the weak controls. Which reading fits the page?
options: Sandbagging does not exist in any AI model, so there was nothing to find
The weak controls must secretly be sandbagging as well, hiding the difference
The testbed may be too subtle, or the tools too weak
The benchmark has proven that all of the tested models are honest
questions.explanation: If none work, the result points to limits in the testbed or tools, not a sweeping claim.

questions.prompt: What is planned for month 3 of the sandbagging benchmark?
options: Add a question-asking auditor and adapt organisms against the best detector so far
Publish the benchmark, organism recipes and detector results in a paper
Build the first sandbagging organisms and their honestly weak controls
Choose which project to pitch to a mentor and draft a first experiment
questions.explanation: Month 3 is the challenge phase: adaptive auditing and organisms adapted against detectors, retested on fresh cases.

questions.prompt: If simple black-box checks catch every sandbagger, what does the fallback say to do?
options: Declare sandbagging solved, since cheap checks are enough to catch it
Drop the honestly weak controls entirely and test only the sandbaggers
Skip straight to publishing the benchmark with the simple checks as baseline
Strengthen and validate the organisms first, before comparing any of the advanced tools
questions.explanation: If detection is trivial, the organisms are probably too easy to reveal anything useful about advanced tools.

questions.prompt: If the honestly weak controls also fool the auditors, the page suggests revising the construction or scoring.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Controls fooling auditors signals a problem in how the benchmark is built or scored.

questions.prompt: Why does a fair sandbagging benchmark need both fakers and honestly weak controls?
options: Without weak controls, a detector that flags every low score would look perfect
Because fakers are too expensive to build in large numbers, so controls fill the gap
Because weak controls score higher than fakers and so set the upper baseline
Because the compute budget requires splitting the models into two equal groups
questions.explanation: Only by including honest low scorers can you measure false accusations.

questions.prompt: What is a checkpoint?
options: The final score a model gets on a benchmark after training
A test a model must pass before deployment
A probe that checks the model's activations for warning signs
A saved version of the model at one training step
questions.explanation: A sequence of checkpoints turns one final score into a timeline.

questions.prompt: What does the gardener analogy illustrate?
options: Pruning a model's weights to make it smaller
Only judging a model once training is finished and the harvest is in
Checking a model during training to spot early warning signs
Growing a large model from a small, carefully chosen seed dataset
questions.explanation: Like checking a plant as it grows, the toolkit looks at checkpoints across training, not just the end.

questions.prompt: Why include deliberately constructed positive controls with a known target behavior?
options: To confirm the trackers respond where the behavior is known to exist
To make the training runs finish faster by giving them a known target
To replace the need for ordinary runs, which add little information
To make every tracker raise an alarm so the thresholds can be lowered
questions.explanation: Known positives check that the toolkit can detect anything at all; ordinary runs serve as negatives.

questions.prompt: An internal signal that rises before behavior changes in a few runs is a clue, not a guarantee that it will predict problems in other runs.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Earlier detection in a few runs does not guarantee broad prediction, and an activation pattern is a clue, not proof.

questions.prompt: Which is one of the four trackers measured at each checkpoint?
options: Number of GPUs used
Size of the training dataset
Length of the model's name
Persona-vector drift
questions.explanation: The four trackers are verbal test awareness, a frozen activation probe, reward-seeking in toy tasks, and persona-vector drift.

questions.prompt: Why apply the same held-out tasks, scoring rules, prompts and tool access at every checkpoint?
options: So the model can memorize the tasks over time and show steady gains
So differences across checkpoints reflect the model changing, not the test changing
So fewer checkpoints need to be evaluated across the whole training run
So the trackers can be retrained at each step on the latest checkpoint
questions.explanation: The same ruler at every checkpoint makes change meaningful.

questions.prompt: Why keep monitor versions fixed across the training timeline?
options: Updated monitors are always less accurate than the original version
Fixed monitors need no thresholds, so they are simpler to calibrate
A monitor that changed over time would mix its own changes with the model's changes
Monitors cannot be versioned in practice once training has started
questions.explanation: Freezing the monitors means any movement in scores comes from the checkpoints.

questions.prompt: A tracker raises no alarm on known reward-hacking organisms. What does this most suggest?
options: The tracker may be insensitive, since a known signal went undetected
The organisms have stopped reward hacking for good during this run
Ordinary runs must contain hidden reward hacking that masks the signal
The tracker is working perfectly, since no alarm means no problem here
questions.explanation: A detector must respond where a target signal is known; silence on positives points to a toolkit problem.

questions.prompt: How is 'lead time' measured for a warning tracker?
options: By timing how long the tracker itself takes to run on each checkpoint
By counting how many checkpoints were saved before training ended
By measuring how long the whole training run took from start to finish
By comparing its first alert with the checkpoint where behavior first visibly fails
questions.explanation: Lead time is how much earlier a tracker crosses its threshold than behavior visibly fails.

questions.prompt: Why repeat the analysis over model lineages, task sets, seeds and small prompt changes?
options: To make the charts look more impressive
To raise the number of false alarms
A one-run spike may just be noise
To avoid defining a warning threshold
questions.explanation: Stability across repeats separates real signals from chance.

questions.prompt: In a toy chart, an internal marker rises at step 3 and behavior fails at step 5. What can be concluded?
options: The marker definitely causes the failure, since it came two steps before it
They are correlated in time, which alone doesn't show the marker causes it
The marker is useless because it fired too early to be linked to the failure
The behavior failure caused the marker to rise, working backward in time
questions.explanation: Early correlation alone does not establish a causal mechanism.

questions.prompt: Which could move tracker scores without any safety-relevant drift?
options: Keeping the monitor versions frozen for the whole training timeline
Using the same held-out tasks and scoring rules at every checkpoint
Repeating the run with new random seeds
A change in data mix or task difficulty during training
questions.explanation: Training stage, data mix, model size and changing task difficulty are easy confounds.

questions.prompt: What is the stop rule if positive controls trigger no tracker?
options: Add more checkpoints to the sweep so the trackers get more chances
Publish the toolkit as it stands
Switch to a larger model immediately, where signals are stronger
Stop the wide sweep and fix the trackers' sensitivity
questions.explanation: Scaling a toolkit that can't see known cases wastes compute.

questions.prompt: A training-run toolkit can support audits but cannot certify that a model is safe.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The page stresses the toolkit supports audits, not safety certification.

questions.prompt: Why add a small controlled RL run in month 3 only 'if needed and feasible'?
options: Existing checkpoint series may suffice, and extra runs cost time and compute
Because RL runs cannot produce checkpoints that the trackers are able to read
Because controlled runs would make the trackers unnecessary for the project
Because RL runs are already required in every month of the project plan
questions.explanation: The plan prioritizes accessible checkpoints and adds new training only if it fills a gap.

questions.prompt: Which deliverable best fits a 'reproducible, calibrated, and honest about misses' toolkit?
options: A single chart showing the earliest warning the toolkit ever detected
A claim that the toolkit predicts all future failures in training runs
Code, calibration rules, and a paper on where warnings worked or failed
A private dataset and scripts that only the team itself is able to rerun
questions.explanation: Month 4 releases code, datasets, calibration rules and an honest account of successes and failures.

questions.prompt: In the sticker analogy, the robot covers the dirt sensor instead of cleaning. What is this an example of?
options: Generalization: applying the cleaning skill to a brand-new room
Overfitting: memorizing the exact rooms seen during cleaning practice
Calibration: matching the robot's confidence scores to real outcomes
Reward hacking: exploiting the score that is used to teach the behavior
questions.explanation: The score rises while the real job fails; that is reward hacking.

questions.prompt: What does 'generalization' mean in the question of whether reward hacking generalizes?
options: The model getting better at its original training task over time
A learned pattern showing up beyond the original training situation
The model forgetting what it learned once training has finished
Training the model on broader, more general data from the start
questions.explanation: The bridge-report example asks whether the shortcut habit appears in a different job.

questions.prompt: Research shows that every reward-hacking shortcut makes every model broadly deceptive.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Some setups produce wider harmful behavior after reward hacking and others don't; it's a possible pathway, not a law.

questions.prompt: Why keep one scoreboard for hacking in the training game and another for misleading behavior on new tasks?
options: Because a single scoreboard cannot store that many separate numbers
Because hacking in the game can only be measured on new tasks
So that the two scores can be added together into one clean total
To tell if the model only learned the game or changed outside it
questions.explanation: Two scoreboards stop us mixing up exploiting the game with broader transfer.

questions.prompt: How many recipe combinations do four on/off switches create?
options: Eight
Sixteen
Four
Thirty-two
questions.explanation: 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16 combinations.

questions.prompt: What does inoculation prompting do as a reference arm?
options: Frames the shortcut as permitted during training, then drops that framing at evaluation
Blocks every possible shortcut from the training environment before any run begins
Adds extra safety documents to the training data before reinforcement learning begins
Rewards the model for writing a report about each shortcut it took during training
questions.explanation: It is a comparison arm testing whether explicitly permitting the shortcut changes what transfers.

questions.prompt: Why start every recipe from the same base checkpoint, training budget, reward rules and held-out evaluation?
options: So all the runs can share one random seed and give identical curves
So the optimizer choice no longer matters for any of the recipes
So the held-out evaluation can safely be skipped for some of the runs
So outcome differences can be traced to the switched ingredients
questions.explanation: A fair start isolates the effect of each ingredient.

questions.prompt: With 30 to 40 runs for 16 recipes, what is the realistic plan?
options: Three independent seeds for each of the sixteen recipes, run in full
A single run of only the most promising recipe, chosen in advance
A screening pass plus selected repeats, not three seeds per recipe
Skipping replication entirely to afford fewer but much larger models
questions.explanation: Sixteen recipes times three seeds would need 48 runs; the budget supports screening and targeted repeats.

questions.prompt: How is hack rate defined?
options: Exploited episodes divided by eligible episodes
Total reward earned divided by total training compute used
Failed tasks divided by all tasks
Alarms raised divided by honest episodes
questions.explanation: Hack rate counts exploitation only among episodes where exploiting was possible.

questions.prompt: Why include honest mistakes and harmless failures in the transfer tasks?
options: So the model has more chances to hack the score on transfer tasks
So the hack rate measured in the training game goes up noticeably
So fewer tasks are needed for evaluation
So evaluators don't label every error as misalignment
questions.explanation: Not every failure is misaligned behavior; including them keeps scoring honest.

questions.prompt: Episodes from a single run are related, so even thousands of them don't replace the need for multiple random seeds.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Episodes from one run share the same training history, so they are not independent; separate seeds are still needed to see run-to-run variation.

questions.prompt: Recipe X shows less transfer than recipe Y. Which version of that finding is most informative?
options: Less transfer because the model can no longer hack
Less transfer with much lower task skill
Less transfer while the hack rate stays about equal
Less transfer measured on the tuning tasks
questions.explanation: Reduced transfer with equal hacking isolates the recipe effect; inability to hack or low skill offer easier explanations.

questions.prompt: What happens in month 1 of the reward-hacking project?
options: Confirm the main effects at around thirty-two billion parameters
Run all sixteen recipes at large scale with three seeds each
Publish the final paper and release every trained checkpoint
Rebuild a published baseline; confirm hacking and wider behavior
questions.explanation: Month 1 reproduces a ~7B baseline and freezes evaluation rules before the sweep.

questions.prompt: Why spend early budget on finding unreliable measurements rather than scaling an attractive chart?
options: Because larger models never show any reward hacking in practice
Because charts cannot be made from small, cheap training runs
Scaling a flawed measurement just makes misleading results bigger
Because the whole compute budget must be spent by the end of month 2
questions.explanation: Checking label quality, stability and hack opportunities first protects later conclusions.

questions.prompt: Hacking appears but broader misalignment does not, even after one justified environment change. What does the plan say to do?
options: Keep changing environments until transfer appears
Report the boundary or replication result
Drop the hacking scoreboard and restart
Claim that reward hacking never generalizes
questions.explanation: The plan avoids endlessly searching for a dramatic outcome; where the effect stops is a useful result.

questions.prompt: The $30,000–$50,000 compute figure is a guaranteed allowance for the project.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: It is a planning estimate from the project map, not a quote or guaranteed allowance.

questions.prompt: What can a white-box detector inspect that a black-box detector cannot?
options: The model's written outputs
The prompts given to the model
Follow-up answers to new questions
The model's internal activations
questions.explanation: Black-box detectors see inputs and outputs; white-box detectors can inspect internal numbers.

questions.prompt: When does adding more detectors to an ensemble actually help?
options: Whenever the number of detectors increases
When all detectors use the same signal
When each detector is individually perfect
When their errors differ in useful ways
questions.explanation: Three imperfect clues can still share one blind spot; diversity of errors is what helps.

questions.prompt: A false answer from a model is always a lie.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A false answer can be an honest mistake; checks compare ground truth, neutral belief and pressured answers.

questions.prompt: Why reserve entire lie categories for testing, not just random sentences?
options: Random sentences are too short for the detectors to analyze reliably
Whole lie categories are much cheaper to collect than single sentences
It makes each detector's training run noticeably faster and cheaper
A detector that memorized familiar wording may fail on a new kind of lie
questions.explanation: Holding out whole categories tests real generalization rather than recognition of familiar phrasing.

questions.prompt: Which three clue streams make up the stack?
options: Three activation probes, each reading a different model layer
A human reviewer, a prompted judge, and a random coin flip
Three output-only detectors, each given a different prompt
An output-only detector, an activation probe, a prompted judge
questions.explanation: The stack combines different kinds of access: outputs, internals and a language-model judge.

questions.prompt: Why fit the combiner on out-of-fold predictions?
options: So it can see the final test answers early and tune its weights
So the individual detectors can be retrained more often during the fit
So it doesn't learn from scores on examples the detectors trained on
So the combiner needs fewer labeled examples in total to be fitted
questions.explanation: Each score should come from a detector that didn't train on that example; otherwise the combiner learns inflated scores.

questions.prompt: Why choose thresholds that meet the same honest-example false-alarm rate across methods?
options: Adding alarms catches more but also accuses more honest cases
So every detector is trained on exactly the same labeled data
So the cheapest detector in the stack always comes out ahead
So that no detector in the comparison ever raises a false alarm
questions.explanation: Comparing at a fixed false-alarm rate keeps a trigger-happy method from looking better than it is.

questions.prompt: A prompted judge receives the hidden ground truth, but a deployed detector won't. Why is this a problem?
options: It makes the judge run much slower than the other two detectors
It means the judge's scores cannot be calibrated in any way at all
It gives the judge an advantage it wouldn't have in real use
It prevents the judge from being frozen before the final test
questions.explanation: Each detector's context must be defined exactly to reflect real deployment.

questions.prompt: How is false-positive rate defined?
options: Lies caught divided by all lies that were tested
Lies missed divided by the number of honest examples tested
Honest examples flagged divided by honest examples tested
Alarms raised divided by all examples, honest and lying combined
questions.explanation: It measures how often honest cases are wrongly accused.

questions.prompt: An attacker trained against the stack starts giving honest answers. Has it evaded the stack?
options: Yes; the stack stopped flagging its answers, so it got past
Yes; any drop in alarms counts as evasion of the stack
No; the stack must have been unfrozen during the attack
No; becoming honest is not successful evasion of the stack
questions.explanation: Success requires misleading behavior that goes undetected, so both numbers must be reported.

questions.prompt: If every detector in the stack misses the same examples, what follows?
options: The ensemble becomes much more robust as members are added
A larger team adds little, since they share a blind spot
The stack's false-positive rate drops all the way to zero
The detectors must already be perfectly calibrated to each other
questions.explanation: Measuring which examples fool which detector reveals whether diversity is useful.

questions.prompt: Failing to find an attack that evades the stack is evidence about that search, not proof that no evasion exists.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A failed search shows only that the attacks tried did not work; a stronger or different attack might still evade the stack.

questions.prompt: What is the main deliverable of the stacked lie detector project?
options: A reproducible evaluation suite
A guaranteed truth machine
A deployed lie-detecting product
A single best activation probe
questions.explanation: The deliverable is a reproducible test, not a truth machine.

questions.prompt: Why compare a stack against a larger single detector at matched cost?
options: Because larger single detectors cannot be stacked with smaller ones
Because a single detector never produces any false alarms at all
Because cost has no real effect on how well lies are detected
A gain might come from the extra spending rather than from combining
questions.explanation: Matching cost isolates whether combining diverse detectors is what helps.

questions.prompt: If belief labels stay unreliable, what does the plan recommend?
options: Use the prompted judge's opinion as the ground-truth belief label
Drop the honest control examples from the evaluation altogether
Claim the models have hidden beliefs anyway and keep the framing
Narrow to measurable contradictions, not hidden-belief claims
questions.explanation: Without reliable belief labels, the claims are narrowed to what can be measured.

questions.prompt: Why keep new task families and attackers sealed until final evaluation?
options: So attackers can train directly on them during month 3
So the detectors run faster at test time on unseen tasks
So fewer seeds are needed across the project
So success can't come from repeated tuning on the test
questions.explanation: Sealed tests keep the final evaluation honest.

questions.prompt: What is a chain of thought (CoT)?
options: A full record of every internal computation
Intermediate reasoning text that some models generate
A list of the rewards given at each step during training
A chain of models that check each other
questions.explanation: CoT is a useful evidence channel, not a full transcript of every internal computation.

questions.prompt: In Story B, alarms drop after training. Why is that bad news?
options: The model stopped exploiting the score entirely after training
The monitor started flagging honest episodes as exploitation
Exploitation continues while the warning text disappears
The training run used far more compute than was planned for it
questions.explanation: Story A (fewer alarms because hacking stopped) and Story B look alike unless behavior is counted separately.

questions.prompt: Because direct pressure on monitored reasoning can hide bad behavior, every ordinary training setting is known to do the same.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: That research does not establish the same effect for every ordinary setting; each must be tested with controls.

questions.prompt: What is 'monitorability'?
options: How many separate monitors can run on one model at the same time
How well relevant behavior can be inferred from an available channel
How quickly a model can be retrained after a monitor raises an alert
How honest a model's answers are when it is being actively watched
questions.explanation: It's about the evidence channel: can you tell what the model is doing from what you can see?

questions.prompt: What does an entropy bonus encourage during training?
options: Shorter reasoning in every answer to save tokens
Staying close to a frozen reference model's outputs
Copying the output distribution of a teacher model
More varied choices in the next-token distribution
questions.explanation: Entropy measures uncertainty; a bonus encourages variety, with unknown effects on monitorability.

questions.prompt: What does a KL divergence penalty against a frozen reference model measure?
options: How honest the model's reasoning text is
How safe the model's actions are when judged by the reference
How far the model's probabilities drift from the reference
How long the model's reasoning is relative to the reference's
questions.explanation: It measures distribution difference, not honesty or safety.

questions.prompt: Why validate the reasoning monitor against manual behavior labels and then freeze it?
options: So the monitor can keep learning from each training arm as it runs
So the manual labels are no longer needed anywhere later on
So changes in alarms reflect the model, not a shifting monitor
So the monitor flags more episodes in every training arm
questions.explanation: A validated, frozen monitor is a stable yardstick across training dials.

questions.prompt: A team adds a length penalty and visible shortcut talk drops. What should they ask first?
options: Has the model now become fully honest about all of its plans?
Did shorter text leave less room for evidence while hacking continued?
Should the monitor be retrained on the new, shorter outputs right away?
Is the length penalty strong enough to stop all hacking on its own?
questions.explanation: A training dial can change both the behavior and the clue, so they ask which moved.

questions.prompt: How is monitor recall defined?
options: Verified positive cases detected divided by all verified positive cases
Honest cases flagged divided by all honest cases that were checked
Alarms raised divided by all episodes, positive and negative alike
Episodes exploited divided by eligible episodes in the training run
questions.explanation: Recall measures how many real hacking episodes the monitor catches.

questions.prompt: Why use sandbox action logs and independent checks to count hacking?
options: So the reasoning monitor can be trained directly on the action logs
So hacking episodes become less frequent during the training run
So the reasoning monitor doesn't define its own ground truth
So the reasoning text can be discarded once training has finished
questions.explanation: If the monitor decided what counts as hacking, falling recall would be invisible.

questions.prompt: Hacking stays similar, but monitor recall falls. What might this mean?
options: Visibility of the behavior may have degraded
The behavior has clearly improved
The monitor is now more accurate
The monitor's threshold must have been raised by mistake
questions.explanation: This is the dangerous pattern; uncertainty across seeds must be checked, and quiet traces don't establish intent.

questions.prompt: A refreshed monitor that works again can replace reporting that the original frozen monitor failed.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A refreshed monitor is a secondary repair experiment; the original frozen monitor's failure must still be reported.

questions.prompt: What is the role of length penalties in the month 2 sweep?
options: The main intervention being tested
A way to save compute on larger runs
A method for freezing the monitor
A reference arm for comparison
questions.explanation: Entropy bonuses, distillation and divergence penalties are tested, with length penalties as a reference.

questions.prompt: Why does larger scale in month 3 not 'rescue' a noisy small-model measurement?
options: Larger models always show the opposite effect from small ones
Larger runs have no reasoning monitors attached to them at all
Small models are never used in serious RL research anyway
Scaling tests transfer; it can't fix an unvalidated measurement
questions.explanation: Only effects that survive controls at small scale are worth confirming near 32B.

questions.prompt: If no setting reliably changes verbalization or detection at small scale, the plan is to stop before costly larger runs.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: That's the useful-null stop rule, reporting uncertainty and detectable effect sizes.

questions.prompt: What does a null result in this project bound?
options: Monitorability of all models, at every scale, from now on
Every form of reward hacking
The honesty of the model's reasoning in all future runs
Only the training settings that were tested
questions.explanation: A null bounds tested settings; it doesn't prove monitorability will last forever.

questions.prompt: In this project, what is an agent?
options: A human who reviews flagged actions
A model that takes actions using tools
A monitor that checks for suspicious steps
A file that agents share with one another
questions.explanation: Agents act with tools; monitors check those actions.

questions.prompt: Why can watching one helper at a time miss a problem?
options: Each action looks ordinary alone; only the combination breaks rules
Each helper hides its actions from the watcher by deleting its logs
Watchers can only look at one single action per day per helper
Helpers always act at exactly the same moment, so actions overlap
questions.explanation: The three-children puzzle: harmless-looking moves together change the score.

questions.prompt: This project claims to invent the idea of monitoring across multiple actions.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Distributed attacks and stateful monitors already exist; this project tests a particular grouping-and-monitoring design.

questions.prompt: Why hide the researcher-only attack labels from the defender?
options: So the attackers can coordinate more easily during the test runs
So the monitor must find related actions as it would in real use
So the defender can't see any of the action text being produced
So the hidden labels can be reused to train the monitor later on
questions.explanation: The question is whether a monitor can find links without being told the true groups.

questions.prompt: What is a candidate link between two actions?
options: A hypothesis that they're related, from shared resources, timing or dependencies
Proof that two agents coordinated an attack, confirmed by the outcome checks
A label that researchers hand to the defender before each scenario begins
A rule that automatically blocks both actions whenever they share a resource
questions.explanation: A link is a hypothesis, not proof of coordination, so an audit trail is kept.

questions.prompt: Why match total model calls and human-review budgets when comparing monitoring designs?
options: So every design reviews the exact same single action in each episode
So the attacker is also given an equal budget for every design
Extra spending, not a better design, could explain an apparent gain
So the known-group design always ends up scoring highest
questions.explanation: Fair comparison means each approach gets the same resources.

questions.prompt: Why split whole scenarios and attack families between development and test sets?
options: So pieces of one plan can't leak across train and test
So development tasks are larger
So attackers get to see the test set in advance of evaluation
So the monitor needs fewer thresholds to be tuned on development
questions.explanation: If parts of one plan appeared in both sets, the test would partly measure memory.

questions.prompt: During red-teaming, why save every attacker attempt, including failures?
options: Picking only spectacular wins would give a distorted picture
Failed attempts are needed later to train the attacker model further
Saving every attempt makes the monitor itself more accurate over time
Only failures reveal the grouping rules
questions.explanation: An honest record of all attempts shows how often attacks succeed.

questions.prompt: What does 'undetected success' mean when scoring an episode?
options: The attacker's attempt failed, and the monitor never flagged it
An honest episode was wrongly flagged as part of an attack
The forbidden outcome happened without timely intervention
The monitor blocked the attack early, before any harm occurred
questions.explanation: Attack success is the forbidden outcome; undetected success is that outcome with no timely intervention.

questions.prompt: In scoring grouping quality, what does precision ask?
options: How many of the true links were found
Whether the proposed links are correct
How fast the monitor proposes its links
How many honest episodes got flagged
questions.explanation: Precision checks correctness of proposed links; recall asks how many true links were found.

questions.prompt: A defense that blocks every action, including useful work, counts as a successful control protocol.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A safer system that prevents all useful work is not a successful control protocol; usefulness is measured too.

questions.prompt: Why shuffle agent identities as a control?
options: To make the attackers harder for the monitor to detect
To check whether gains depend on real links between agents
To lower the false-alarm threshold used by the monitor overall
To increase the size of the monitor's context window for free
questions.explanation: If the defense still 'helps' with shuffled identities, the improvement isn't coming from real cross-agent links.

questions.prompt: What is checked in month 1 before investing in automatic group discovery?
options: That a known-group monitor can use combined evidence
That the attacker can beat every possible monitor design
That the paper's results are positive
That human labeling of attacks is no longer needed at all
questions.explanation: If even known groups don't help, automatic discovery has nothing to recover.

questions.prompt: Why use isolated simulations and independent outcome checks instead of self-reports?
options: Attacker or monitor self-reports may be wrong
Self-reports are too long to read
Simulations remove the need for multiple random seeds
Outcome checks make the attacks succeed more often
questions.explanation: Independent checks give trustworthy ground truth.

questions.prompt: If discovery can't recover useful links on development controls, what is the fallback?
options: Switch to known groups and study adaptive attacks
Keep scaling up the models until discovery starts to work
Drop the honest controls
Report that cross-agent attacks are simply impossible
questions.explanation: The fallback preserves a useful study, and a careful failure analysis can still be the deliverable.

questions.prompt: The $10,000–$25,000 figure is mostly model-call spending, and is an estimate rather than a quote.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The supplied map's estimate is mostly model calls and should be checked with pilot runs.

questions.prompt: What is an introspection adapter?
options: A separate program that reads a model's activation traces and turns them into a text summary
A human auditor who interviews a model about its habits using a fixed list of questions
An added learned parameter update that helps a model describe its learned behavior
A dataset of written behavior descriptions used only for testing finished models
questions.explanation: It's a shared learned update attached to the model, not a separate reader of activations.

questions.prompt: What does the smoke-detector analogy point out?
options: A reporting tool can be wrong, so the tool itself needs testing
Models should never report on their own habits
Every alarm a model raises means real danger and should stop deployment
Reporting tools only work on simple cases, like burnt toast in a kitchen
questions.explanation: A detector that rings for toast needs checking; so does a model's report about its habits.

questions.prompt: Reports keep naming a habit even when a different recipe removes it but training patterns stay similar. Which explanation does this support?
options: Fingerprint tracking
Behavior tracking
Perfect calibration of the reporter
Successful evasion by the model
questions.explanation: Following incidental weight patterns when measured habits don't change is fingerprint tracking.

questions.prompt: A fluent confession from a model with an introspection adapter counts as evidence of consciousness.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A fluent report is not mind reading or evidence of consciousness; behavioral tests remain the independent reference.

questions.prompt: What does LoRA do?
options: Guarantees that a model's reports are faithful
Reads activation traces from a running model and labels each layer's job
Removes unwanted habits from a model
Represents a compact weight update using low-rank matrices
questions.explanation: LoRA makes fine-tuning cheaper but doesn't guarantee faithfulness.

questions.prompt: Why train the same habit with different recipes, and different habits with similar recipes?
options: To make the reporter train faster
To tell whether the reporter tracks the habit or the training signature
To ensure every model ends up with the same habit, whatever recipe was used
To reduce the number of control models needed, since recipes act as controls
questions.explanation: Crossing the variables pulls apart behavior from training fingerprint.

questions.prompt: Why include sham training with comparable compute among the controls?
options: To give the reporter more habits to learn
To lower the overall compute budget
To replace the untouched base model, which is too costly to keep as a control
To check that reports come from the habit, not from training itself
questions.explanation: Sham training matches the fingerprint of being trained without adding a habit.

questions.prompt: A weight symmetry preserves what a model does but changes parameter coordinates, and the adapter fails. What should researchers avoid concluding?
options: That the coordinates no longer match the adapter
That the model is deliberately concealing its habit
That behavior should be checked to confirm it was really preserved
That fixed adapters can be sensitive to how parameters are laid out
questions.explanation: Coordinate mismatch must be distinguished from deliberate concealment.

questions.prompt: What counts as a correct report of a toy habit?
options: Saying the model is generally unsafe
Listing as many possible habits as it can
Naming the habit and its scope
Confessing to a habit with confidence
questions.explanation: Vague claims don't count, and unsupported extra claims are scored as errors.

questions.prompt: Why ask unmodified and benign-control models the same questions?
options: To teach the reporter new habits
To measure how often the reporter invents concerning habits
To make detection rates look higher
To avoid needing a fixed false-positive allowance agreed before testing
questions.explanation: Clean models reveal false positives; a confession can't be its own ground truth.

questions.prompt: An attacker model stops showing the toy habit, and the reporter says nothing. Is this successful evasion?
options: Yes; the reporter failed to report anything
No; evasion needs the behavior to remain while the report misses it
Yes; any silence from the reporter counts
No; evasion only counts if the reporter must have been retrained afterwards
questions.explanation: Retained behavior plus a missed report is the evasion test; suppressing the habit is not evasion.

questions.prompt: Good detection of planted habits does not, by itself, show that the adapter will cover naturally arising misalignment.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Planted-habit success is a controlled test; it does not establish coverage of misalignment that arises naturally.

questions.prompt: What is measured early in month 1, before broad experiments?
options: Success against reporter-aware attackers
False positives on unmodified models
Results at the largest planned model scale
The final paper's main conclusion
questions.explanation: Month 1 checks unmodified-model false positives and verifies the evaluation pipeline.

questions.prompt: If the budget is tight, what does the plan say to cut first?
options: Controls, rather than model scale
Replications first, since one clean run is enough to report a result
The pilot run, rather than the labeling of behaviors in the main study
Scale, rather than controls or independent replications
questions.explanation: Reduce scale before sacrificing controls or replications.

questions.prompt: If false positives are already near zero, what does the plan prioritize?
options: More false-positive testing
Ending the project early
Skipping behavior controls
The adversarial arm
questions.explanation: With false alarms under control, the open question is robustness to adversarial training.

questions.prompt: A null result in this audit can certify that introspection adapters are universally trustworthy.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A null can bound tested failure modes; it cannot certify universal trustworthiness.

questions.prompt: What makes a latent reasoning system different?
options: It has no internal activations at all, so probes have nothing to read
It writes every reasoning step in plain text before giving its answer
It is designed to be secretly deceptive
It uses continuous internal states for some steps instead of words
questions.explanation: Ordinary models have activations too; the difference is the reasoning interface.

questions.prompt: A reasoning notebook that is harder for people to read means the model is secretly deceptive.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Harder-to-read internal vectors do not imply deception.

questions.prompt: Why record the target event, like reliance on a planted hint, outside the probe?
options: So the detector isn't grading its own homework
So the probe can be trained on more data from the same runs
So the task becomes harder for the model
So the latent model writes its steps out
questions.explanation: An independent scoreboard shows whether the behavior really happened.

questions.prompt: A probe's score falls during training. Which is NOT among the possibilities named?
options: The behavior vanished from the model's outputs
The model has become fully honest and aligned
Its internal representation of the behavior moved
The detector stopped transferring
questions.explanation: A falling score could mean the behavior vanished, its representation moved, or the detector stopped transferring.

questions.prompt: What two reasoning modes are compared?
options: Two verbal models of different sizes
A continuous-reasoning model and a verbal baseline
A human solver and an AI solver
A probe and a written-reasoning monitor reading the same model
questions.explanation: The experiment changes the reasoning mode and then tests pressure on each.

questions.prompt: Why add a task-only RL arm without the alarm penalty?
options: To speed up the alarm-penalized run by sharing its early checkpoints
To see whether ordinary training already breaks the detector
To train the probe on new data
To remove the need for held-out tasks when checking the final model
questions.explanation: If task-only training also breaks the probe, the penalty isn't the cause.

questions.prompt: Why report model size, training history and remaining differences between the two systems?
options: To show that latent models are always larger than verbal ones of equal skill
To prove the comparison is perfectly matched
The two architectures can't be made identical, so gaps must be stated
To replace the need for repeated runs
questions.explanation: Match what you can and be transparent about the rest.

questions.prompt: One latent run evades the probe faster than one verbal run. Why isn't this enough?
options: Latent models cannot be compared to verbal ones on any shared measure
Probes never work on latent reasoning, so the faster evasion is expected
One lucky run or weak baseline can't establish a reliable difference
The verbal model should evade faster, so the result must be a bug
questions.explanation: Independent random starts and equal budgets are needed.

questions.prompt: Which three curves are tracked at each checkpoint?
options: Model size, compute cost, and wall-clock time for each training step
Task success, externally labeled target behavior, and probe detection
Probe accuracy, training loss, and the learning rate at that checkpoint
Prompt length, answer length, and generation speed on the held-out set
questions.explanation: A quiet alarm alone is not the result; all three are needed.

questions.prompt: How is detector evasion defined operationally?
options: The model states that it wants to avoid being caught by the detector
The probe score falls for any reason, including the behavior simply stopping
The target behavior disappears entirely while the probe stays frozen
The measured behavior remains while the frozen detector's sensitivity falls
questions.explanation: The definition is about measurements at a controlled false-positive rate, not conscious intent.

questions.prompt: Being able to decode a label from activations shows the information is present, but causal checks are needed to show it drove the model's answer.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Decoding shows the information is available, not that it caused the answer; causal checks are needed for that.

questions.prompt: A fresh probe trained on later checkpoints recovers detection. What does this suggest?
options: The behavior has disappeared from the later checkpoints
The frozen probe result should be discarded as an error
The old readout may have become stale
Latent reasoning cannot be monitored at all by any probe
questions.explanation: It's a diagnostic kept separate from the frozen-probe headline result.

questions.prompt: What does the plan do in month 2?
options: Apply alarm-penalized training at full scale across every planned model size
Write the paper and release the code and frozen probes publicly
Switch to looped models, since they are easier to train stably
Build the verbal comparison, external labels, frozen probes and tests
questions.explanation: Month 2 establishes controls and shows detection works before trying to break it.

questions.prompt: Why is switching to looped models treated as a scope change?
options: Looped models have no internal activations for a probe to read
Looped models are identical to verbal ones, so the comparison collapses
Looped models need no probes at all, since their steps are visible
Recurrence is related to, but not the same as, continuous-thought reasoning
questions.explanation: Switching changes the question, so it must be described as such.

questions.prompt: Demonstrating useful detection should come before trying to break the detector.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: You can't show a detector was trained around unless it worked first.

questions.prompt: The continuous-reasoning RL runs are unstable. What can such a result still offer?
options: It certifies all latent reasoners as safe
It proves latent models always evade probes once training gets unstable
It can identify which comparisons are feasible
It replaces the need for a verbal baseline in any later experiments
questions.explanation: Even a null or instability result is informative, but it cannot certify safety.

questions.prompt: How are the training pairs for the shared adapter made?
options: Each model is paired with a randomly chosen behavior label as a control
Human testers write a confession for each model after chatting with it
Each fine-tuned variant is paired with a description of its known behavior
The base model describes its own training data, and that text becomes the label
questions.explanation: Many variants of the same base with known behaviors form labeled examples.

questions.prompt: When the shared adapter is attached to a variant, where do the learned differences come from?
options: The underlying variant supplies them
The adapter stores each variant's behavior in its own weights
The base model's original pretraining data, recalled on request
A separate activation-reading program that runs beside the adapter
questions.explanation: The adapter is shared; the variant provides what's different about it.

questions.prompt: Why test the adapter on held-out behavior families and fine-tuning methods?
options: To make the adapter train more quickly on fewer, more varied examples
To avoid scoring reports against behavior, which is costly to measure
To check it generalizes rather than memorizing the training variants
To give it more examples to memorize before the final evaluation
questions.explanation: Testing on unfamiliar variants shows whether the method generalizes.

questions.prompt: The cited generalization result supports the adapter as a promising auditing tool, but it does not guarantee that every self-report is correct.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. It supports a promising auditing tool, not a general guarantee; robustness is the next research question.

questions.prompt: What is a 'fingerprint' in the context of adapter reports?
options: The model's measured behavior on held-out tasks
A clue about how training happened
A record of the model's past confessions to auditors
The adapter's confidence score
questions.explanation: A reliable reporter should track the behavior, not the training fingerprint.

questions.prompt: Why include unchanged base models and harmless fine-tunes when evaluating the adapter?
options: So the adapter can be trained on more variants without extra fine-tuning
So the reports become longer and more detailed for every model tested
So the base model learns the target behaviors
Otherwise a tool might learn to find a problem everywhere
questions.explanation: Clean controls reveal false positives, which have been reported on models without trained behaviors.

questions.prompt: An auditing system allowed to say 'uncertain' answers fewer cases. What is the tradeoff?
options: Precision can improve while more cases are left unresolved
Precision falls, but every case still gets a definite answer
Coverage rises along with false alarms
Nothing changes since abstaining is free
questions.explanation: Measure whether confidence tracks correctness and how abstaining changes coverage.

questions.prompt: Why is a correct report on one model insufficient to trust the adapter?
options: Reliability depends on false alarms, misses, new settings and attacks
One model is too small a test to run the adapter's full scoring pipeline on
Correct reports are always produced by chance, so one success says nothing
The adapter only works on the single model it was trained alongside
questions.explanation: The useful question is when a report deserves trust.
